_comment: The Phase 6 performance gate (issue #165, EPIC B #81's performance contract).
#81 says API p95 and transfer throughput should stay within 'approximately
10%' of baseline. 'Approximately 10%' is not a gate, so #165 owns turning it
into numbers a later run can pass or fail without argument: one benchmark
host, one workload, and one threshold per gated metric.
Every number here is derived from measurement, not chosen. Two independent
five-capture baselines were taken on the host below and compared against each
other; the observed capture-to-capture movement of each median is what sets
whether a metric is gated on a ratio alone, on a ratio plus an absolute noise
floor, or reported without a gate. docs/perf/README.md shows that comparison
and the reasoning for each line.
_required_metrics_comment: The seven metrics EPIC B #81's performance contract names. A baseline record
missing any one of them is incomplete and check-baseline.sh refuses it, so a
--skip-image capture can never be mistaken for a real baseline.
_thresholds_comment: Gated metrics. direction=lower_is_better uses max_ratio, higher_is_better uses
min_ratio. noise_floor_abs, where present, is a second condition that must
ALSO be exceeded before the metric fails: it exists only for metrics whose
absolute value is small enough that a 10% budget is inside measured machine
noise, and its value is set from that measurement rather than picked.
Read a floor as the binding condition rather than as a rounding allowance.
Two conditions that must both hold means the WIDER one is what is enforced,
and on a sub-millisecond metric the floor is normally the wider one. The
metric's own "why" says which condition binds and what the budget therefore
is in practice.
A ratio here is not a promise that the metric can resolve 10%. Each one is
sized from that metric's own measured movement, so they differ by an order
of magnitude: image_size_bytes carries 1.05 because two builds of one commit
are byte-identical and precision is the only thing setting it, while
transfer_mb_per_second carries 0.60 because one unchanged tree spans 1.398x
across machine conditions (#635). That is one rule producing two very
different numbers, not an exception. Read each metric's "why" for what its
gate can and cannot catch before treating a pass as evidence.
Metrics deliberately NOT gated: startup_to_healthy_ms (12.0% median-to-median
movement between two identical captures, so a 10% gate would fail against an
unchanged tree), idle_cpu_percent and idle_cpu_seconds_total (the process is
below the measurement floor at idle), and the two p50s (recorded as context
for their p95s). Those are recorded, reported and reviewed, not gated;
claiming to gate a number that cannot hold still would be worse than saying
plainly that it is a review signal.

api_read_p95_ms.why: the API p95 EPIC B #81 names. Measured median-to-median movement between two identical five-capture baselines was 0.019 ms (14.6%), so the ratio alone is inside noise at this magnitude, and the 0.05 ms floor is 2.6x that movement. Both conditions must hold before this metric fails, so what is enforced is the wider of the two, not the 1.10: against the 0.168 ms baseline the ratio allows 0.185 ms and the floor allows 0.218 ms, so the floor always binds and the effective budget is +29.8%. (It was +38.5% against the 0.130 ms baseline this record replaced in #635; the floor is absolute, so a larger baseline narrows the effective budget rather than widening it, and this sentence moves with the record because a threshold's justification that quotes a number the record no longer holds is the same defect the metric below it exists to catch.) That is wider than the regression this floor was sized against. An added loopback proxy hop was later measured at 0.047 ms at p95 on this host, which is just under the floor, so this gate cannot catch that hop. Closing that needs a quieter measurement before the floor can come down, not a smaller number written over the same noise. docs/perf/README.md carries the arithmetic, and scripts/perf/selftest.sh pins which condition binds with one control either side of the floor.

transfer_mb_per_second.why: the transfer throughput EPIC B #81 names. The 0.93% median-to-median movement this was originally sized on is a real number that measures the wrong quantity, and #635 established that: both of those baselines were taken back to back on a QUIET machine, so what they measured is repeatability under one condition rather than sensitivity to condition, and a 256 MiB disk-to-disk copy is the metric here most exposed to the difference. Six runs of one unchanged tree on 2026-09-08 under a load average of 11 to 12 gave 479.584, 492.995, 619.020, 624.583, 651.716 and 670.434 MB/s: a spread of 1.398x with nothing changed, against a 0.90 ratio that allows 1.11x. All six were below the 672.180 floor a 0.90 ratio sets on the recorded 746.867, and one of the six was below the 483.932 floor the PREVIOUS baseline set, so this is a property of the metric rather than of either capture. A gate that goes red on an unchanged tree teaches everyone to ignore it, which is the same rule that left startup_to_healthy_ms ungated at 12% movement. This metric stays gated because #81 names it, and it takes the treatment api_read_p95_ms already got for the same tension: the threshold is widened from measurement and what it really enforces is written down rather than left implied. 0.60 puts the floor at 448.120 MB/s, 7.0% below the worst of the six, because six samples at one load level do not locate the tail and fitting the threshold to the worst one observed (0.64 leaves 0.3%) would repeat the mistake the 0.93% figure made. What that buys is a gate against the structural regression class and not a marginal one: it still refuses a halving, which is what scripts/perf/selftest.sh mutates, and it will not notice a 20% loss. Read that as the honest capability of this metric on this host, not as a target. No noise_floor_abs, unlike api_read_p95_ms: that floor exists because a sub-millisecond number sits near its own measurement resolution, whereas this quantity is large and varies multiplicatively, so a ratio is the right instrument and a second condition nobody could reason about would only widen an already wide rule. Capture this metric on a quiet machine; docs/perf/README.md carries the measurements and what to do when it fails.

idle_rss_bytes.why: EPIC B #81 requires material idle-memory growth attributable solely to the refactor to be explained and approved. Measured median-to-median movement was 0.22%, so a 10% budget is roughly forty-five times the noise.

config_write_p95_ms.why: the configuration write path. Measured median-to-median movement was 4.8%, so the 10% budget has only about two times headroom: the tightest of the gated metrics, and the one most likely to need a re-measurement rather than a fix if it trips.

image_size_bytes.why: two independent builds of the same commit produced byte-identical image sizes, so there is no noise to allow for. 5% is a real gate, and it is far below the cost of the specific regression #81 forbids, adding a production Node server to host the web UI.
